extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in political economy, public finance, and institutional design
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on designing and funding public works (roads, canals, harbours) and on organising the administration of justice to minimize corruption and economic harm. Covers financing mechanisms, management structures, and institutional safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation and independence of judiciary from executive
rubrics_metrics.description: The judicial should be separated from the executive power and rendered as much as possible independent of that power; the judge should not be liable to be removed from his office according to the caprice of the executive, nor should the regular payment of his salary depend upon its good will or economy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judicial is united with executive, justice is frequently sacrificed to politics; independence preserves individual liberty and the sense of security. Institutional safeguards include secure tenure and salary arrangements not controlled by the executive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition of judicial presents and appointment of fixed salaries
rubrics_metrics.description: It was commonly stipulated that no present for the administration of justice should, under any pretence, be accepted either by the sovereign, or by his bailiffs and substitutes, the judges; fixed salaries were appointed to the judges, supposed to compensate them for the loss of ancient emoluments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Banning direct presents to judges reduces corruption. Fixed salaries help, but do not obviate other necessary payments (lawyers/attorneys will still be paid by parties). The method of paying salaries must itself be independent of executive whim to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and centralisation of court fees to prevent corruption
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the fees of court are paid all at once, at a certain period of every process, into the hands of a cashier or receiver, to be by him distributed in certain known proportions among the different judges after the process is decided and not till it is decided, there seems to be no more danger of corruption than when such fees are prohibited altogether.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collect fees centrally and distribute only after decision; make shares known and proportioned (e.g., by hours/days employed). This reduces incentives to corrupt decision-making and can encourage diligence because reward follows performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fees of court may legitimately fund the administration of justice if well-regulated
rubrics_metrics.description: The fees of court seem originally to have been the principal support of the different courts of justice... Those fees, without occasioning any considerable increase in the expense of a law-suit, might be rendered fully sufficient for defraying the whole expense of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: User-fee funding can be equitable and self-sustaining when fees are precisely regulated, paid appropriately, and distributed to incentivise diligence; poor regulation or executive capture undermines this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid per-page or quantity-based payment schemes for attorneys/clerks
rubrics_metrics.description: It has been the custom in modern Europe to regulate, upon most occasions, the payment of the attorneys and clerks of court according to the number of pages which they had occasion to write... the attorneys and clerks have contrived to multiply words beyond all necessity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pay structures that reward volume (pages, lines) incentivise verbosity and unnecessary work, corrupt legal language, and increase costs. Prefer payment methods that reward substantive work/outcome instead of mechanistic counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stamp-duties or court levies risk multiplying proceedings and creating perverse incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: A stamp-duty upon the law proceedings of each particular court, to be levied by that court, and applied towards the maintenance of the judges, ... The judges, indeed, might in this case, be under the temptation of multiplying unnecessarily the proceedings upon every cause, in order to increase, as much as possible, the produce of such a stamp-duty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Funding mechanisms that flow directly to the court create incentives to expand jurisdiction or create artificial proceedings. Avoid revenue collection schemes tied to volume of procedure without checks and balances.

rubrics_metrics.name: User-pay tolls proportional to use (weight/tonnage) are the most equitable way to fund transport infrastructure
rubrics_metrics.description: A highway, a bridge, a navigable canal, for example, may, in most cases, be both made and maintained by a small toll upon the carriages which make use of them... they pay for the maintenance of those public works exactly in proportion to the wear and tear which they occasion of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tolls charged in proportion to weight/tonnage allocate costs to those who cause wear and ultimately fall on consumers in proportion to benefit; because public works lower transport costs, consumers typically gain overall. Design tolls to match marginal wear/use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not convert maintenance user-tolls into general revenue (regressivity warning)
rubrics_metrics.description: A tax upon carriages, in proportion to their weight, though a very equal tax when applied to the sole purpose of repairing the roads, is a very unequal one when applied to any other purpose... it is chiefly paid by the consumers of coarse and bulky, not by those of precious and light commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If user-tolls are diverted to general state needs, they become regressive and harm production/commerce; governments may be tempted to raise such tolls, which would narrow markets and discourage heavy-goods production. Keep use-tolls ring-fenced for maintenance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build public works only where commerce requires them and scale to ability to pay
rubrics_metrics.description: When high-roads, bridges, canals, etc. are in this manner made and supported by the commerce which is carried on by means of them, they can be made only where that commerce requires them... Their expense, too, their grandeur and magnificence, must be suited to what that commerce can afford to pay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructing magnificent works in locations lacking commerce; match location and scale of works to demonstrable demand and capacity to finance them (through tolls or local revenue) to prevent waste and vanity projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate ownership/management form by infrastructure type (private canals vs. public roads)
rubrics_metrics.description: In several different parts of Europe, the toll or lock-duty upon a canal is the property of private persons, whose private interest obliges them to keep up the canal... The tolls for the maintenance of a highroad cannot, with any safety, be made the property of private persons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Canals (which become unusable if neglected) are better suited to private toll ownership because private owners have strong maintenance incentives; highways (which remain passable when neglected) are ill-suited to private toll proprietorship and should be under commissioners/trustees with oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local/provincial funding and administration better for works whose convenience is locally confined
rubrics_metrics.description: Even those public works, which are of such a nature that they cannot afford any revenue for maintaining themselves, but of which the conveniency is nearly confined to some particular place or district, are always better maintained by a local or provincial revenue, under the management of a local and provincial administration, than by the general revenue of the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use local revenue streams and local management for district-limited works to ensure proper maintenance and local accountability rather than central executive control, which may neglect unglamorous but useful local projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trustees and commissioners require proper selection and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: If mean and improper persons are frequently appointed trustees; and if proper courts of inspection and account have not yet been established for controlling their conduct, and for reducing the tolls to what is barely sufficient for executing the work to be done by them; the recency of the institution both accounts and apologizes for those defects, of which, by the wisdom of parliament, the greater part may, in due time, be gradually remedied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governance arrangements for bodies managing tolls/works must include competent appointments, inspections, accounts, and parliamentary or judicial oversight to prevent overcharging, wasteful spending, and slovenly execution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of executive centralisation absorbing local works priorities
rubrics_metrics.description: In the progress of despotism, the authority of the executive power gradually absorbs that of every other power in the state, and assumes to itself the management of every branch of revenue which is destined for any public purpose... the proud minister of an ostentatious court, may frequently take pleasure in executing a work of splendour and magnificence ... but to execute a great number of little works ... is a business too mean and paltry to merit the attention of so great a magistrate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Central executive control biases towards spectacular projects visible at court and neglects numerous small but highly useful local works. Preserve decentralised decision-making and evaluation criteria to match local needs rather than central prestige.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer stable, appropriate dedicated funds for sustaining institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: That fund might arise from the rent of landed estates, the management of each estate being entrusted to the particular court which was to be maintained by it. That fund might arise even from the interest of a sum of money... The necessary instability of such a fund seems, however, to render it an improper one for the maintenance of an institution which ought to last for ever.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose funding sources that are stable and suited to the institution’s permanence; some dedicated funds (estate rents, interest) can work but may be unstable and thus inappropriate for perpetual institutions like courts—evaluate long-term reliability.
